notes.text: Latitude: Angular distance north or south of the Equator.
Longitude: Angular distance east or west of the prime meridian.
Equator: The zero-degree parallel dividing northern and southern hemispheres.
Prime meridian: The zero-degree longitude passing through Greenwich.
International Date Line: The approximate 180-degree boundary across which calendar dates change.
Rotation: Earth spinning on its axis.
Revolution: Earth travelling around the Sun.
Axial tilt: The inclination of Earth's rotational axis relative to its orbital perpendicular.
Equinox: An occasion when day and night are approximately equal worldwide.
Solstice: An occasion when the Sun reaches its greatest northward or southward apparent position.
Map scale: The ratio of map distance to actual ground distance.
Contour line: A line joining points of equal elevation.
Isobar: A line joining places of equal atmospheric pressure.
Isotherm: A line joining places of equal temperature.
Isohyet: A line joining places receiving equal rainfall.
Cartography: The study and practice of making maps.
Topographic map: A map showing relief and detailed natural and human features.
Globe: A three-dimensional model of Earth.
Remote sensing: Obtaining information about Earth's surface without direct physical contact.
GIS: A computer system for storing and analysing geographically referenced data.
GPS: A satellite-based system for determining position.
Standard time: Time adopted for a region from a selected reference meridian.
Local solar time: Time determined by the Sun's apparent position at a longitude.
Tropic of Cancer: The northern tropical parallel at about 23.5 degrees north.
Tropic of Capricorn: The southern tropical parallel at about 23.5 degrees south.
Arctic Circle: The northern polar parallel at about 66.5 degrees north.
Antarctic Circle: The southern polar parallel at about 66.5 degrees south.
Great Circle: A circle whose plane passes through Earth's centre.
Hemisphere: One half of Earth divided by a great circle.
Altitude: Height above a reference level such as mean sea level.
Lithosphere: The rigid crust and uppermost mantle.
Asthenosphere: The relatively weak upper-mantle zone below the lithosphere.
Plate tectonics: The movement and interaction of lithospheric plates.
Convergent boundary: A boundary where tectonic plates move towards each other.
Divergent boundary: A boundary where tectonic plates move apart.
Transform boundary: A boundary where plates slide horizontally past each other.
Subduction: One tectonic plate sinking beneath another.
Fold mountain: A mountain formed mainly by compression and folding of rocks.
Rift valley: A depressed block of land between faults.
Horst: An uplifted block of land bounded by faults.
Volcano: An opening through which molten rock and gases reach the surface.
Magma: Molten rock beneath Earth's surface.
Lava: Molten rock after it reaches Earth's surface.
Epicentre: The surface point vertically above an earthquake focus.
Focus of an earthquake: The point inside Earth where rupture starts.
Seismograph: An instrument that records earthquake waves.
Weathering: The breakdown of rock at or near the surface without transport.
Erosion: The wearing away and removal of material by moving agents.
Deposition: The laying down of transported sediment.
Mass wasting: The downhill movement of material under gravity.
Alluvial fan: A fan-shaped sediment deposit where a stream leaves a steep slope.
Delta: A depositional landform commonly built near a river mouth.
Estuary: A tidal river mouth where fresh water mixes with seawater.
Meander: A winding bend in a river channel.
Oxbow lake: A curved lake formed when a river meander is cut off.
Floodplain: A low-lying river-side surface built mainly by alluvial deposition.
Natural levee: A raised sediment bank beside a river channel.
Gorge: A deep narrow valley with steep sides.
Waterfall: A steep vertical or near-vertical drop in a stream channel.
Watershed divide: A ridge or high ground separating drainage basins.
Drainage basin: The area drained by a river and its tributaries.
Tributary: A stream that joins a larger river.
Distributary: A channel that branches away from a main river.
Glacier: A persistent mass of ice moving under its own weight.
Cirque: An amphitheatre-shaped hollow excavated at a glacier's head.
Moraine: Material deposited directly by a glacier.
U-shaped valley: A broad steep-sided valley shaped by glacial erosion.
Fjord: A sea-flooded glacial valley.
Drumlin: An elongated hill formed from glacial deposits.
Loess: A deposit of fine wind-blown silt.
Barchan: A crescent-shaped sand dune.
Yardang: A wind-eroded streamlined ridge in a dry region.
Deflation: The removal of loose particles by wind.
Karst: Limestone terrain shaped mainly by solution.
Stalactite: A mineral deposit hanging from a cave ceiling.
Stalagmite: A mineral deposit growing upward from a cave floor.
Sinkhole: A surface depression caused by dissolution or collapse in soluble rock.
Sea arch: An opening eroded through a coastal headland.
Sea stack: An isolated rock pillar left offshore by coastal erosion.
Spit: A narrow coastal sediment ridge attached to land at one end.
Tombolo: A sediment bar connecting an island to the mainland.
Lagoon: A shallow water body separated from the sea by a barrier.
Continental shelf: The gently sloping submerged edge of a continent.
Continental slope: The steeper descent beyond a continental shelf.
Abyssal plain: A broad relatively flat area of the deep ocean floor.
Ocean trench: A long narrow deep depression in the ocean floor.
Mid-ocean ridge: A submarine mountain system associated with seafloor spreading.
Atoll: A ring-shaped coral reef enclosing a lagoon.
Igneous rock: Rock formed by cooling and solidification of molten material.
Sedimentary rock: Rock formed by deposition and consolidation or precipitation.
Metamorphic rock: Rock altered by heat or pressure without complete melting.
Rock cycle: The processes that transform rocks among different types.
Fossil: A preserved remain or trace of ancient life.
Continental drift: The long-term movement of continents relative to one another.
Pangaea: The proposed ancient supercontinent joining most major landmasses.
Weather: The short-term state of the atmosphere at a place.
Climate: The long-term pattern of weather in a region.
Troposphere: The lowest atmospheric layer where most weather occurs.
Stratosphere: The atmospheric layer containing most of the ozone layer.
Mesosphere: The atmospheric layer in which many meteors burn up.
Thermosphere: A high atmospheric layer whose temperature increases strongly with height.
Insolation: Incoming solar radiation received by Earth.
Albedo: The fraction of incoming radiation reflected by a surface.
Terrestrial radiation: Long-wave radiation emitted by Earth.
Conduction: Heat transfer through direct molecular contact.
Convection: Heat transfer by the movement of a fluid.
Advection: Horizontal transport of properties such as heat by moving air.
Lapse rate: The rate at which air temperature changes with height.
Temperature inversion: A condition in which temperature rises with height through a layer.
Atmospheric pressure: The force per unit area exerted by the weight of air.
Pressure gradient: The change in atmospheric pressure over distance.
Coriolis effect: The apparent deflection of motion caused by Earth's rotation.
Trade winds: Persistent tropical winds blowing towards the equatorial low-pressure belt.
Westerlies: Prevailing mid-latitude winds blowing broadly from west to east.
Polar easterlies: Cold high-latitude winds blowing broadly from east to west.
ITCZ: The tropical convergence zone where trade winds meet and air rises.
Jet stream: A narrow band of strong winds high in the atmosphere.
Monsoon: A seasonal reversal in prevailing wind direction.
Sea breeze: A daytime wind blowing from sea towards warmer land.
Land breeze: A night-time wind blowing from land towards warmer sea.
Valley breeze: Daytime upslope air movement in a mountain valley.
Mountain breeze: Night-time downslope movement of cooled air.
Humidity: The amount of water vapour present in air.
Relative humidity: The percentage ratio of actual to saturation water-vapour content at a temperature.
Dew point: The temperature at which air becomes saturated on cooling.
Condensation: The change of water vapour into liquid water.
Sublimation: The direct change between solid and gaseous states.
Evaporation: The change of liquid water into water vapour.
Transpiration: The loss of water vapour from plants.
Evapotranspiration: Combined water loss by evaporation and plant transpiration.
Orographic rainfall: Rainfall caused by air rising over a relief barrier.
Convectional rainfall: Rainfall produced by the uplift of strongly heated air.
Frontal rainfall: Rainfall caused when air rises along a boundary between air masses.
Rain shadow: A relatively dry area on the leeward side of a mountain barrier.
Cyclone: A low-pressure system with inward-moving winds.
Anticyclone: A high-pressure system with outward-moving winds.
Eye of a tropical cyclone: The relatively calm central region of a mature tropical cyclone.
Storm surge: An abnormal rise of seawater level caused mainly by a storm's winds and pressure.
El Nino: Abnormal warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean.
La Nina: Abnormal cooling of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean.
Western disturbance: An eastward-moving weather system bringing winter rain to northwestern India.
Loo: A hot dry summer wind of the north Indian plains.
Kalbaisakhi: A pre-monsoon thunderstorm common in Bengal and neighbouring regions.
Mango showers: Pre-monsoon showers associated with parts of southern India.
Retreating monsoon: The seasonal withdrawal phase of the southwest monsoon.
Continentality: A large seasonal temperature range associated with distance from the sea.
Maritime influence: The moderating effect of nearby oceans on temperature.
Greenhouse effect: Warming caused by atmospheric absorption and re-emission of infrared radiation.
Urban heat island: Higher urban temperatures relative to surrounding rural areas.
Microclimate: The climate of a small local area.
Drought: A prolonged shortage of available water relative to normal needs.
Heatwave: A period of unusually high temperature for a location and season.
Cloudburst: An exceptionally intense short-duration rainfall event over a small area.
Salinity: The concentration of dissolved salts in water.
Tide: The periodic rise and fall of sea level driven mainly by lunar and solar gravity.
Spring tide: A tide with a larger tidal range around new or full moon.
Neap tide: A tide with a smaller tidal range around quarter moon.
Ocean current: A persistent directed movement of seawater.
Upwelling: The rise of deeper water towards the ocean surface.
Thermohaline circulation: Large-scale ocean circulation driven by density differences from temperature and salinity.
Gulf Stream: A warm Atlantic current flowing away from the Gulf of Mexico region.
Labrador Current: A cold current flowing southward along northeastern North America.
Humboldt Current: A cold current flowing along western South America.
Canary Current: A cool current flowing along northwestern Africa.
Kuroshio Current: A warm current in the northwestern Pacific.
Oyashio Current: A cold current in the northwestern Pacific.
Benguela Current: A cold current along southwestern Africa.
Agulhas Current: A warm current along southeastern Africa.
Tsunami: A series of long waves caused by major displacement of water.
Hydrological cycle: The continuous circulation of water among land oceans and atmosphere.
Infiltration: The entry of surface water into soil.
Percolation: The downward movement of water through soil and rock.
Aquifer: A permeable geological formation capable of storing and transmitting groundwater.
Water table: The upper surface of a saturated groundwater zone.
Artesian well: A well in a confined aquifer where water rises under pressure.
Watershed management: Coordinated conservation of land and water in a drainage area.
Rainwater harvesting: Collecting and storing rainfall for later use or groundwater recharge.
Desalination: Removing dissolved salts from saline water.
Ecosystem: Organisms interacting with one another and their physical environment.
Habitat: The natural place where an organism lives.
Ecological niche: The functional role and resource use of a species in an ecosystem.
Population: Individuals of one species living in an area.
Community: Populations of different species living and interacting in an area.
Biodiversity: The variety of life at genetic species and ecosystem levels.
Endemic species: A species naturally restricted to a particular geographical area.
Invasive alien species: A non-native species whose spread causes ecological or other harm.
Keystone species: A species with an unusually large ecological effect relative to its abundance.
Flagship species: A species used to raise public support for conservation.
Umbrella species: A species whose protection can help conserve many co-occurring species.
Indicator species: A species whose presence or condition reflects environmental quality.
Food chain: A sequence of organisms through which food energy passes.
Food web: A network of interconnected food chains.
Trophic level: A feeding position in a food chain.
Producer: An organism that makes organic food from inorganic substances.
Primary consumer: An organism that feeds directly on producers.
Decomposer: An organism that breaks down dead organic matter.
Detritus: Dead organic material and associated waste.
Ecological pyramid: A representation of numbers biomass or energy across trophic levels.
Carrying capacity: The population an environment can sustain over time.
Ecological succession: A directional change in community composition over time.
Primary succession: Community development on a surface without established soil.
Secondary succession: Community recovery after disturbance where soil remains.
Climax community: A relatively stable late-successional community under prevailing conditions.
Mutualism: An interaction in which both participating species benefit.
Commensalism: An interaction benefiting one species without a major effect on the other.
Parasitism: An interaction benefiting one organism while harming its host.
Predation: An interaction in which one organism kills and eats another.
Competition: An interaction arising from the shared use of limited resources.
Bioaccumulation: The build-up of a substance within an organism over time.
Biomagnification: Increasing concentrations of a persistent substance at higher trophic levels.
Eutrophication: Nutrient enrichment that can cause excessive aquatic plant and algal growth.
Biochemical oxygen demand: The oxygen microbes require to decompose organic material in water.
Acid rain: Precipitation made unusually acidic by pollutants such as sulphur and nitrogen oxides.
Photochemical smog: Polluted air formed by sunlight-driven reactions involving nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons.
Particulate matter: Tiny solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in air.
Carbon sink: A system that absorbs more carbon than it releases over a period.
Carbon sequestration: The capture and long-term storage of carbon.
Carbon footprint: The greenhouse-gas emissions attributable to an activity or entity.
Ecological footprint: An estimate of biologically productive area needed to support resource use and wastes.
Afforestation: Establishing forest on land not recently forested.
Reforestation: Restoring forest cover to previously forested land.
Social forestry: Tree-growing programmes involving communities and local needs.
Agroforestry: Combining trees with crops or livestock on the same land.
In-situ conservation: Protecting species in their natural habitats.
Ex-situ conservation: Protecting species outside their natural habitats.
Biosphere reserve: An area combining conservation with sustainable development and research.
Wildlife corridor: A habitat link allowing animals to move between larger habitat areas.
Buffer zone: An area around a protected core that moderates external impacts.
Ecotone: A transition zone between ecological communities.
Edge effect: A change in species composition or conditions at a habitat boundary.
Wetland: An area where water saturation strongly shapes soils and living communities.
Mangrove: A salt-tolerant tree or shrub community of tropical tidal coasts.
Coral bleaching: Loss of symbiotic algae or pigments from stressed corals.
Desertification: Land degradation in drylands due to climatic and human factors.
Land degradation: A reduction in land's productive or ecological quality.
Sustainable development: Development meeting present needs without undermining future generations' needs.
Circular economy: An economic approach that retains material value through reuse repair and recycling.
Composting: The biological decomposition of organic waste into a useful soil amendment.
Vermicomposting: Composting that uses earthworms to process organic matter.
Bioremediation: Using living organisms to remove or reduce environmental pollutants.
Phytoremediation: Using plants to remove stabilise or transform contaminants.
Polluter pays principle: The principle that polluters should bear pollution-control and damage costs.
Precautionary principle: Taking protective action despite scientific uncertainty where serious harm is plausible.
Environmental impact assessment: A process for evaluating likely environmental effects before approving a project.
